I drift off into a world of my own

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette: Kofi had always been a gentle soul, with a love for books and people that served him well in his role as a librarian. But it was on a fateful day, twenty years ago, when his life took a drastic turn. He was caught in the midst of a terrorist attack at a crowded market in Lagos, where he had gone to buy gifts for his family. The sounds of gunfire and screams still echoed vividly in his mind, as did the image of a young boy lying motionless on the ground. The anniversary of that day always brought back a flood of emotions, making Kofi anxious and irritable. He would avoid talking about it with anyone, even his wife, afraid of being overwhelmed by memories he couldn't shake off. People misbehaving in public - littering, pushing, or being generally inconsiderate - also triggered a sense of outrage in him, transporting him back to the chaos of that day. As time passed, Kofi found himself drifting away from social gatherings and events that might bring him joy. He would rather stay home, lost in his own thoughts, than risk being confronted with triggers that could set off a chain reaction of memories. He became withdrawn, avoiding crowded places like shopping centers or public events, where the noise and chaos felt too much to bear. Kofi's memories of the attack were still crystal clear - he could recall every detail, from the smell of smoke to the sound of sirens in the distance. They played over and over in his mind like a film, making it hard for him to concentrate on anything else. Sometimes, something as innocuous as a loud noise or a certain smell would instantly bring back the full memory without warning, leaving him feeling disoriented and shaken. His wife noticed the change in him, but Kofi couldn't explain why he was withdrawing from life. He knew it wasn't rational - after all, he had survived the attack, and his family was safe. But the fear of being overwhelmed by memories kept him trapped in a cycle of avoidance. The more he avoided positive events and social interactions, the more his memories seemed to haunt him. As the years went by, Kofi became increasingly isolated. His job at the library, which had once brought him so much joy, now felt like a chore. He would find himself zoning out during conversations with patrons, lost in thoughts of that fateful day. His wife tried to be patient, but even she couldn't understand why he was still struggling after all these years. Kofi's fantasies of escape became more elaborate over time - he would imagine himself in a quiet, peaceful world, far away from the trauma of his past. But when reality snapped him back into place, he felt lost and disoriented once again. The cycle of avoidance and memory replay seemed to have no end, leaving Kofi feeling stuck and helpless. It was only when his wife sat him down and gently asked if he needed help that Kofi realized he couldn't keep living in this state of limbo. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he wanted to try - for himself, for his wife, and for the life they once shared together. As he sat there, surrounded by the silence of their home, Kofi finally felt a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, he could find his way back to living again.
